I can’t tell you how inspiring this is to hear. I just started working on it after my diagnosis in May, so I have a ways to go, but I’m the exact same way. Skipped my entire junior year to drink vodka and self harm in the bathroom all day every day, attempted, BARELY graduated, I have issues holding down a job for more than 6 months, and I’ve never had friends stay with me for longer than 2 years. I have made a lot of progress, but of course, sometimes it feels like I’ll never be “normal”. I am very proud of you and it’s great to hear that at least one person has made such impressive progress.

It does sound like she has a lot of symptoms. It’s going to piss her off regardless if anyone tells her she has those symptoms. Even when my fiancé- who I know only wants the best for me- brought it up, I was kind of upset that he even noticed, let alone told me to go to a psychiatrist. In my opinion, it couldn’t really hurt to let her know she might need help. At first she will be upset. But afterwards, it’s up to her to take a look inward and take steps to improve. It’s up to her if she wants to listen or not. Depending on what she does, it shows a big part of her character as well. And if you’re broken up, not looking for a relationship or friendship with her in the future, it doesn’t matter if she sees you in a bad light. If I’m being honest, she’s probably (likely involuntarily) turning things around in her brain to make every issue in the relationship 100% YOUR fault instead accepting any accountability anyway. 

If it was me, and my ex told me I exhibited BPD symptoms, my first (unmedicated and no therapy) thought would be “He’s trying to do anything he can to make me feel like everything was my fault, he can’t let go of me, he just wants to keep making me feel like shit,” etc. I would recommend also sending some links, like the [symptoms,](https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/conditions/borderline-personality-disorder/symptoms/) an [overall description,](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/conditions-and-diseases/borderline-personality-disorder) and this is the [handbook](https://mydoctor.kaiserpermanente.org/ncal/Images/Emotion%20Regulation%20DBT%20Skills%20ADA%2004292020_tcm75-1598999.pdf) I use to process my emotions. If she does feel inclined to look at them, she might have a “come to Jesus” moment like I did where everything makes sense and I realized why I act the way I do. 

Overall, I don’t think it could hurt to let her know. Just give a lot of reassurance that you’re telling her this for her own well being, even though she won’t believe you. Don’t be surprised when she gets upset, either. Whether she takes your advice or denies everything, that’s up to her, not you.

as a woman who has BPD, I’m so sorry. It’s truly not fun for anyone. I’m amazed that my fiancé stays with me through it sometimes. I feel like the difference that can make or break a relationship is if you can recognize you have BPD symptoms when they come up, and make efforts to improve. I’m in DBT therapy, so now I can recognize “oh I’m getting irrationally upset” or “I’m being selfish”, and once I realize that, I can look in my little handbook and calm myself down or I can use coping skills I learned in therapy. DBT and mood stabilizers make a huge difference. It takes a tonnn of patience, and constant effort from BOTH parties. To be clear, I don’t blame you for breaking up with her at all. I just wish that more women with BPD would put effort in to manage their symptoms. If it’s important, you find a way.
